accuracy.evidence: Follows the National Curriculum wording for upper key stage 2 (identify main ideas drawn from more than one paragraph and summarise them) and lower key stage 2 (retrieve and record information from non-fiction), and CCSS RI.3.2 to RI.5.2. Hedgehog facts (nocturnal, 5,000 to 7,000 spines, hibernation roughly November to March, up to 2 km a night) and bat facts (roosts, insects, echolocation) match standard wildlife-trust guidance.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips at this age: giving the topic or one vivid detail as the main idea (tray cards tagged whole and one, quiz tags topic and tiny), treating any true fact as a key detail (step 2 prediction and odd-sentence rounds), summaries that copy, add opinion or retell one paragraph (sort tags copy, view, detail; quiz tags part and opinion), and notes copied as whole sentences (bin row).

lab_distinct.evidence: flaggist is a reading-process lab: a paragraph with a main-idea drop box, a tap-the-odd-sentence round, a summary builder that grows as sentences are kept, a bats notes table with a bin row, and a choose-how-to-record step. flagnfind teaches book features, not summarising or note-taking, and the shingle gate passed against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step makes the child do the comprehension move rather than read about it: choosing between the main idea, one detail and the bare topic for four paragraphs, rejecting a true but off-point sentence, deciding what a summary keeps, and filing key words into a table while binning a copied sentence and an opinion. The summary box shows the three kept sentences, so the child sees a short summary form.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions carry tempting wrong options: the narrow detail They eat slugs as paragraph 2's main idea, every true fact counting as a key detail, and a summary being about as long as the text. Each is tested inside its own step by the cards, the odd-sentence rounds and the summary that ends at three sentences, and the done message reports what the child predicted.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions with tagged wrong answers (tiny, topic, part, opinion, copyall, steps, offtopic), each explaining why that choice misses, such as a summary needing the main point of each paragraph rather than one. In-lab feedback also names the slip: a card is only one detail, Hedgehogs is the article topic, a note copies a whole sentence, or a picked recording method suits a different task.

readability.evidence: The kid explanation passes the family FK limit in the validator, using short sentences and one hedgehog example carried across all four paragraphs. The adult text sits inside the 10.5 limit and lists the key terms for ages 7 to 10. Lab paragraphs are three short sentences each and the cards are a few words, so a seven-year-old can read them with help.

no_filler.evidence: Kid paragraphs each teach one idea (main idea, key detail, summary, notes) with a concrete hedgehog or recording example. Adult paragraphs give curriculum placement, terms, named mistakes and what each lab step practises. Practice and mastery items test choosing main ideas, key details, summary sentences, notes and recording methods on new texts, not recall of definitions.

mobile.evidence: Checked screenshots at 360 px Android dark and iPhone 13 light for all six steps: the paragraph, main-idea box and three tray cards fit one screen, the summary and leave-out zones stay above the sentence card, the table rows show labels and notes without overlap after widening the bin label, and the three recording tiles fit in one row. Show me finished every task on iPhone 13 in the browser gate.

accessibility.evidence: The browser gate's axe-core run found no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light or dark theme on desktop or iPhone 13 and logged no console errors. Every drag or tap on the canvas has a labelled button twin (choose a main idea, pick a sentence, keep or leave out, file a note in a row, choose a recording method) and the canvas aria-label is rewritten with each result, so feedback never relies on colour.
